title: Old Faithful
photo: Old Faithful Geyser Yellowstone / Yellowstone National Park bison / Upper Geyser Basin Yellowstone
p: Yellowstone became the world's first national park in 1872.
黄石在1872年成为世界上第一个国家公园。
Most of the park is in the state of Wyoming.
公园的大部分位于怀俄明州。
Under the ground, there is very hot rock, so the water there gets hot too.
地下有非常炽热的岩石，所以那里的水也会变热。
Old Faithful is the park's most famous geyser.
老忠实泉是公园里最有名的间歇泉。
About every hour and a half, it shoots hot water and steam high into the air.
大约每隔一个半小时，它就会把热水和蒸汽高高地喷向空中。
Park rangers can guess the next time, so visitors sit and wait with their cameras.
公园管理员能预测下一次喷发的时间，所以游客们拿着相机坐着等待。
While they wait, they may also see big brown bison walking near the road.
等待的时候，他们还可能看到棕色的大野牛在路边走动。
q: When did Yellowstone become a national park?
How often does Old Faithful erupt?
About every hour and a half
What animal might visitors see near the road?

title: The Lady in the Harbor
photo: Statue of Liberty New York / Liberty Island / Statue of Liberty crown
p: The Statue of Liberty stands on a small island in New York Harbor.
自由女神像矗立在纽约港的一座小岛上。
It was a gift from the people of France to the United States.
它是法国人民送给美国的礼物。
It opened in 1886.
它于1886年落成。
The statue is made of copper.
这座雕像是用铜做的。
At first it was a shiny brown color, but over the years the air and rain turned it green.
起初它是闪亮的棕色，但多年来空气和雨水把它变成了绿色。
In her right hand, the lady holds a torch.
女神右手举着一支火炬。
In her left hand, she holds a tablet with the date July 4, 1776.
她左手拿着一块写着1776年7月4日的书板。
For many people who came to America by ship, she was their first view of their new home.
对于许多乘船来到美国的人来说，她是他们看到新家园的第一眼。
q: Who gave the statue to the United States?
Why is the statue green today?
Air and rain changed the copper
It is made of green stone
What does the statue hold in her right hand?

title: Who Is Big Ben?
photo: Elizabeth Tower Westminster / Big Ben clock face / Palace of Westminster London
p: Many visitors to London want to see Big Ben.
许多去伦敦的游客都想看看大本钟。
They usually point at the tall clock tower next to the River Thames.
他们通常会指着泰晤士河边那座高高的钟楼。
But Big Ben is really the name of the huge bell inside the tower!
但其实“大本”是钟楼里那口巨大的钟的名字！
The tower has its own name, too.
这座塔也有自己的名字。
In 2012, it was named the Elizabeth Tower for Queen Elizabeth II.
2012年，它为纪念女王伊丽莎白二世而被命名为伊丽莎白塔。
The clock has four faces, so people can read the time from every side.
这座钟有四个钟面，所以人们从各个方向都能看到时间。
Every hour, the great bell rings with a deep BONG.
每到整点，大钟就会发出低沉的“咚”声。
People all over Britain listen to it on the radio on New Year's Eve.
新年前夜，全英国的人都会在收音机里听它的钟声。
q: What is "Big Ben" really the name of?
What is the tower called now?
How many faces does the clock have?

title: Hop, Hop, Kangaroo
photo: Red kangaroo Australia / Kangaroo joey in pouch / Kangaroo road sign Australia
p: Kangaroos live only in Australia and nearby islands.
袋鼠只生活在澳大利亚及附近的岛屿上。
They have strong back legs and a long, heavy tail.
它们有强壮的后腿和一条又长又重的尾巴。
They do not walk like us; they hop, and they can move very fast.
它们不像我们那样走路，而是跳着走，而且速度非常快。
The tail helps them keep their balance.
尾巴帮助它们保持平衡。
A baby kangaroo is called a joey.
小袋鼠叫作 joey。
When it is born, it is as small as a bean.
它刚出生时只有一粒豆子那么小。
It lives in its mother's pouch and drinks her milk for months.
它住在妈妈的育儿袋里，喝妈妈的奶，一住就是好几个月。
In Australia, you can see yellow road signs with a kangaroo on them, because the animals often cross the road.
在澳大利亚，你能看到画着袋鼠的黄色路标，因为这种动物经常横穿马路。
q: What is a baby kangaroo called?
Why are there kangaroo road signs in Australia?

title: Teddy's Bear
photo: Theodore Roosevelt / Teddy bear Smithsonian / Clifford Berryman Drawing the Line in Mississippi
p: Theodore Roosevelt was president of the United States from 1901 to 1909.
西奥多·罗斯福在1901年至1909年间担任美国总统。
His nickname was "Teddy."
他的昵称是“泰迪”。
In 1902, he went on a bear hunt in Mississippi.
1902年，他去密西西比州猎熊。
Some men tied a tired old bear to a tree and asked him to shoot it, but he said no.
有人把一头疲惫的老熊绑在树上，让他开枪，但他拒绝了。
A newspaper printed a funny drawing of the story.
一家报纸刊登了一幅关于这件事的有趣漫画。
Soon after, a shop owner in New York made a soft toy bear and called it "Teddy's bear."
不久之后，纽约的一位店主做了一只柔软的玩具熊，取名“泰迪的熊”。
The toy became very popular.
这种玩具变得非常受欢迎。
Today, children all over the world sleep with their teddy bears.
如今，全世界的孩子都抱着泰迪熊睡觉。
q: What did Roosevelt do when he saw the tied bear?
Who made the first "Teddy's bear" in this story?
A shop owner in New York

title: The Stones on the Plain
photo: Stonehenge Wiltshire / Stonehenge summer solstice sunrise / Salisbury Plain
p: Stonehenge is a circle of giant stones in the south of England.
巨石阵是英格兰南部的一圈巨大石头。
People started to build it about 5,000 years ago.
人们大约在5000年前开始建造它。
Some of the stones are taller than two men, and they are very heavy.
有些石头比两个人还高，而且非常沉重。
Many of the smaller stones came from Wales, more than 200 kilometers away.
许多较小的石头来自威尔士，距离这里200多公里。
There were no trucks or machines then, so how did people move them?
那时没有卡车或机器，人们是怎么搬动它们的呢？
Nobody knows for sure.
没有人确切知道。
We do know that the stones line up with the sun.
但我们知道，这些石头与太阳的位置对齐。
On the longest day of summer, many people come to watch the sun rise over the stones.
在夏天白昼最长的那一天，许多人会来看太阳从石头上方升起。
q: When did people start building Stonehenge?
Where did the smaller stones come from?
When do many people come to watch the sunrise there?
On the longest day of summer
On the coldest night of winter

title: A Green Day in March
photo: Chicago River dyed green St. Patrick's Day / St. Patrick's Day parade Dublin / Shamrock
p: March 17 is St. Patrick's Day.
3月17日是圣帕特里克节。
St. Patrick is the patron saint of Ireland.
圣帕特里克是爱尔兰的守护圣人。
On this day, people in Ireland and many other countries wear green clothes.
在这一天，爱尔兰和其他许多国家的人都穿绿色的衣服。
Some people wear a shamrock, a small plant with three leaves.
有些人会佩戴三叶草，一种长着三片叶子的小植物。
There are big parades with music and dancing in Dublin, New York and other cities.
在都柏林、纽约和其他城市都有带着音乐和舞蹈的盛大游行。
In Chicago, workers even make the river bright green for the day!
在芝加哥，工人们甚至会在这一天把河水染成鲜绿色！
Many Americans have Irish families from long ago, so the day is very popular in the United States, too.
许多美国人的祖上来自爱尔兰，所以这个节日在美国也很受欢迎。
q: How many leaves does a shamrock have?
What happens to the river in Chicago?

title: Will Winter End Soon?
photo: Punxsutawney Phil Groundhog Day / Gobbler's Knob Punxsutawney / Groundhog Marmota monax
p: February 2 is Groundhog Day in the United States and Canada.
2月2日是美国和加拿大的土拨鼠日。
A groundhog is a furry brown animal that sleeps under the ground all winter.
土拨鼠是一种毛茸茸的棕色动物，整个冬天都在地下睡觉。
An old story says it can tell us when spring will come.
一个古老的说法认为，它能告诉我们春天什么时候到来。
The most famous groundhog is Punxsutawney Phil, from a small town in Pennsylvania.
最有名的土拨鼠是来自宾夕法尼亚州一个小镇的旁苏托尼·菲尔。
Early in the morning, thousands of people wait in the cold to see him come out.
清晨，成千上万的人在寒冷中等着看它出洞。
If Phil sees his shadow, there will be six more weeks of winter.
如果菲尔看到了自己的影子，冬天就还要持续六个星期。
If he does not, spring will come early.
如果没看到，春天就会提前到来。
Of course, he is not always right, but everyone has fun!
当然，它并不总是猜对，但大家都玩得很开心！
q: Where does Punxsutawney Phil come from?
What does it mean if Phil sees his shadow?

title: The Orange Bridge in the Fog
photo: Golden Gate Bridge fog / Golden Gate Bridge San Francisco / Golden Gate Bridge tower
p: The Golden Gate Bridge is in San Francisco, California.
金门大桥位于加利福尼亚州旧金山。
It opened in 1937.
它于1937年通车。
At that time, it was the longest bridge of its kind in the world.
在当时，它是世界上同类桥梁中最长的。
Its name is "golden," but the bridge is not gold at all.
它的名字里有“金”字，但这座桥根本不是金色的。
Its color is called "International Orange."
它的颜色叫作“国际橙”。
This color is easy to see, and it looks beautiful next to the blue sea and green hills.
这种颜色很醒目，在蓝色大海和绿色山丘的映衬下非常漂亮。
In summer, thick fog often covers the bridge, and sometimes only the tops of its two towers can be seen.
夏天，浓雾经常笼罩大桥，有时只能看见两座桥塔的塔顶。
You can walk or ride a bike across it.
你可以步行或骑自行车过桥。
q: What color is the Golden Gate Bridge?
What often covers the bridge in summer?

title: The Bird That Cannot Fly
photo: Kiwi bird New Zealand / North Island brown kiwi / Kiwi crossing sign New Zealand
p: The kiwi is a small brown bird from New Zealand.
几维鸟是一种来自新西兰的棕色小鸟。
It has wings, but they are very small, and it cannot fly.
它有翅膀，但翅膀非常小，所以它不会飞。
It sleeps in the day and looks for food at night.
它白天睡觉，晚上出来找食物。
The kiwi has a long beak with its nose at the very end.
几维鸟有一个长长的喙，鼻孔就长在喙的最尖端。
It pushes its beak into the ground and smells worms and insects.
它把喙插进泥土里，嗅出蠕虫和昆虫。
The mother lays a very big egg for her size.
按体型来说，鸟妈妈产下的蛋非常大。
The kiwi is a national symbol, and people from New Zealand often call themselves "Kiwis."
几维鸟是国家象征，新西兰人也常常称自己为“Kiwi”。
q: When does the kiwi look for food?
At the end of its beak
What do people from New Zealand often call themselves?

title: Reading the Grand Canyon
photo: Grand Canyon South Rim / Colorado River Grand Canyon / Grand Canyon rock layers
p: Standing at the edge of the Grand Canyon in Arizona, many visitors simply fall silent.
站在亚利桑那州大峡谷的边缘，许多游客会不由得沉默下来。
The canyon is about 446 kilometers long and, in places, more than 1.6 kilometers deep.
这条峡谷长约446公里，有些地方深达1.6公里以上。
It was carved over millions of years by the Colorado River, which still flows along the bottom.
它是由科罗拉多河在数百万年间切割而成的，这条河至今仍在谷底流淌。
To geologists, the canyon walls are like the pages of a giant history book.
在地质学家眼里，峡谷的岩壁就像一本巨大历史书的书页。
Each colored layer of rock was formed in a different period, and the oldest rocks at the bottom are nearly two billion years old.
每一层彩色岩石都形成于不同时期，谷底最古老的岩石已有近20亿年历史。
Fossils of sea creatures in the upper layers show that this dry land was once covered by water.
上层岩石中的海洋生物化石表明，这片干燥的土地曾经被海水覆盖。
The canyon became a national park in 1919, and today millions of people visit each year.
大峡谷于1919年成为国家公园，如今每年有数百万人到访。
Rangers warn hikers that walking down is easy but climbing back up in the summer heat can be dangerous, so they should carry plenty of water.
管理员提醒徒步者，下坡容易，但在夏日酷热中爬回来可能很危险，因此要带足水。
q: What do the sea fossils in the rocks show?
The land was once under water
Fish still live in the walls
The river used to be salty
What do rangers advise hikers to do?

title: Twelve Seconds at Kitty Hawk
photo: Wright Flyer first flight 1903 / Wright Brothers National Memorial / Wright Cycle Company Dayton
p: Orville and Wilbur Wright never finished college, yet they solved one of the greatest puzzles of their time.
奥维尔和威尔伯·莱特兄弟从未读完大学，却解开了他们那个时代最大的难题之一。
The brothers ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, and the money from selling and repairing bikes paid for their experiments.
兄弟俩在俄亥俄州代顿开了一家自行车店，靠卖车和修车赚的钱来支付他们的实验费用。
Working with bicycles also taught them that a rider stays up by constantly balancing, an idea they applied to controlling an aircraft.
和自行车打交道还让他们明白，骑车人是靠不断保持平衡才不会倒下的，他们把这个想法用在了控制飞机上。
They tested their gliders on the windy sand hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.
他们在北卡罗来纳州基蒂霍克附近多风的沙丘上测试滑翔机。
When published data on wings turned out to be wrong, they built their own small wind tunnel and collected new measurements.
当他们发现已发表的机翼数据有误时，就自己造了一个小风洞，重新测量数据。
On December 17, 1903, Orville lay on the lower wing of their engine-powered Flyer and took off.
1903年12月17日，奥维尔趴在他们那架装有发动机的“飞行者号”的下层机翼上起飞了。
The flight lasted just 12 seconds and covered about 37 meters, less than the length of a modern passenger jet.
那次飞行只持续了12秒，飞了大约37米，比一架现代客机的机身还短。
Wilbur flew 59 seconds later that day, and the age of powered flight had begun.
当天晚些时候，威尔伯飞了59秒，动力飞行的时代就此开始。
q: How did the Wright brothers pay for their experiments?
With money from their bicycle shop
With prize money from a contest
Why did they build a wind tunnel?
Published wing data turned out to be wrong
They were asked to by a newspaper
How long did the first flight on December 17, 1903 last?

title: All the World's a Stage
photo: Shakespeare's Globe London / Globe Theatre Southwark interior / Shakespeare's Globe thatched roof
p: In 1599, an acting company that included William Shakespeare built a theater called the Globe on the south bank of the River Thames.
1599年，莎士比亚所在的一个剧团在泰晤士河南岸建了一座名为“环球”的剧院。
Many of his greatest plays, including Hamlet and Macbeth, were first performed there.
他的许多伟大剧作，包括《哈姆雷特》和《麦克白》，都是在那里首演的。
The theater was open to the sky, so performances took place in the afternoon, using daylight.
剧院是露天的，所以演出都在下午进行，借助日光照明。
Tickets were cheap for "groundlings," who stood in the yard right in front of the stage.
站在舞台正前方空地上的“站票观众”票价很便宜。
They ate, drank and shouted at the actors, making the experience far noisier than a modern evening at the theater.
他们边吃边喝，还冲着演员喊叫，使看戏的体验比现代剧院的晚场热闹得多。
In 1613, a cannon fired during a play set fire to the thatched roof, and the building burned down within an hour.
1613年，一场演出中发射的炮火点燃了茅草屋顶，整座建筑在一小时内被烧毁。
A careful reconstruction, Shakespeare's Globe, opened near the original site in 1997.
1997年，一座经过精心复原的“莎士比亚环球剧院”在原址附近开放。
It was the first building allowed to have a thatched roof in London since the Great Fire of 1666, and audiences can still buy standing tickets today.
它是自1666年伦敦大火以来第一座获准使用茅草屋顶的伦敦建筑，如今观众仍然可以买站票。
q: Why were plays at the original Globe performed in the afternoon?
What destroyed the first Globe in 1613?
A fire started by a cannon
What is special about the modern Globe's roof?
It was the first thatched roof allowed in London since 1666
It can be opened and closed
It is the tallest roof in London

title: Born in New Orleans
photo: Preservation Hall New Orleans / Congo Square New Orleans / Louis Armstrong Park New Orleans
p: Many people call New Orleans, Louisiana, the birthplace of jazz.
许多人称路易斯安那州的新奥尔良为爵士乐的发源地。
In the 1800s, the port city was a mix of African, French, Spanish and Caribbean cultures.
19世纪，这座港口城市融合了非洲、法国、西班牙和加勒比的文化。
On Sundays, enslaved Africans gathered in a place called Congo Square to play drums, sing and dance, keeping their musical traditions alive.
每逢周日，被奴役的非洲人会聚集在一个叫“刚果广场”的地方打鼓、唱歌、跳舞，使自己的音乐传统得以延续。
By the early 1900s, local brass bands were mixing blues, church music and marching songs into something new.
到了20世纪初，当地的铜管乐队把布鲁斯、教堂音乐和进行曲融合成了一种新的音乐。
Musicians often improvised, inventing melodies on the spot instead of reading every note from paper.
乐手们经常即兴演奏，当场创作旋律，而不是照着乐谱演奏每一个音符。
Louis Armstrong, who grew up poor in the city, became one of the most famous trumpet players in history.
在这座城市的贫困环境中长大的路易斯·阿姆斯特朗，成为了史上最著名的小号手之一。
Jazz is still part of daily life there.
爵士乐至今仍是当地日常生活的一部分。
At some funerals, a brass band plays slow, sad music on the way to the cemetery and joyful tunes on the way back, as people dance in the street behind it.
在一些葬礼上，铜管乐队去墓地的路上演奏缓慢悲伤的音乐，回来时则演奏欢快的曲调，人们跟在后面在街上跳舞。
q: What happened in Congo Square on Sundays?
Enslaved Africans played music and danced
What does it mean that jazz musicians improvised?
They invented melodies on the spot
They read every note from paper
How does the music change at some New Orleans funerals?
It is sad going to the cemetery and joyful coming back
It is joyful the whole time
There is no music at all
It gets slower on the way back

title: A Garden Under the Sea
photo: Great Barrier Reef aerial / Great Barrier Reef coral / Heart Reef Queensland
p: Off the coast of Queensland, in northeastern Australia, lies the Great Barrier Reef.
在澳大利亚东北部昆士兰州的海岸外，坐落着大堡礁。
It stretches for more than 2,300 kilometers and is made up of about 2,900 separate reefs.
它绵延2300多公里，由大约2900个独立的礁体组成。
It is often called the largest structure on Earth built by living things.
它常被称为地球上由生物建造的最大结构。
Those builders are tiny animals called coral polyps.
这些建造者是一种叫作珊瑚虫的微小动物。
Each polyp makes a hard skeleton, and over thousands of years, countless skeletons pile up to form reefs.
每只珊瑚虫都会形成坚硬的骨骼，经过数千年，无数骨骼堆积起来形成了礁体。
The reef provides a home for thousands of species, from colorful fish to sea turtles and sharks.
这片珊瑚礁为成千上万的物种提供了家园，从色彩斑斓的鱼到海龟和鲨鱼。
However, the reef is under threat.
然而，这片珊瑚礁正面临威胁。
When the ocean becomes too warm, corals push out the tiny algae that live inside them and give them color, a process known as bleaching.
海水过热时，珊瑚会排出生活在体内、赋予它们颜色的微小藻类，这一过程被称为白化。
Bleached corals can recover if the water cools, but repeated heat waves make that harder, so scientists are watching the reef closely.
如果海水降温，白化的珊瑚可以恢复，但反复的热浪让恢复越来越难，所以科学家们正密切关注这片珊瑚礁。
q: What builds the Great Barrier Reef?
Ocean water that is too warm
According to the article, can bleached corals recover?

title: The Festival Nobody Invited
photo: Edinburgh Festival Fringe Royal Mile / Edinburgh Fringe street performer / Royal Mile Edinburgh August
p: Every August, the Scottish capital of Edinburgh fills with comedians, actors, dancers and musicians from around the world.
每年八月，苏格兰首府爱丁堡都会挤满来自世界各地的喜剧演员、演员、舞者和音乐人。
They come for the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, often described as the largest arts festival on the planet.
他们是为爱丁堡艺穗节而来的，这个节日常被称为全世界规模最大的艺术节。
The Fringe began almost by accident.
艺穗节的诞生几乎是个意外。
In 1947, a new international festival was launched in the city, but eight theater groups that had not been invited turned up anyway.
1947年，这座城市创办了一个新的国际艺术节，但有八个没有受到邀请的剧团还是来了。
They performed on the "fringe," or edge, of the official event, and the name stuck.
他们在官方活动的“边缘”演出，这个名字从此就沿用了下来。
Its key rule is still that anyone with a show and a venue can take part; there is no committee that selects performers.
它最重要的规则至今仍是：只要有节目、有场地，任何人都能参加；没有委员会来挑选演员。
As a result, you might see a famous comedian in a large theater and then a student play in a tiny room above a pub on the same day.
因此，你可能同一天里既在大剧院看到知名喜剧演员，又在酒吧楼上的小房间里看到学生演的戏。
On the Royal Mile, the city's old main street, performers hand out flyers and put on free shows to attract audiences.
在城市古老的主街皇家英里大道上，表演者们派发传单、免费表演来吸引观众。
w: （名称）沿用下来（stick 的过去式）
q: The Queen ordered a new festival
A pub owner held a contest
Who can perform at the Fringe?
Anyone with a show and a venue
Only groups chosen by a committee
What do performers do on the Royal Mile?
Hand out flyers and give free shows

title: At the Edge of an Empire
photo: Hadrian's Wall Northumberland / Housesteads Roman Fort / Vindolanda tablets
p: Nearly 1,900 years ago, the Roman Emperor Hadrian ordered a wall to be built across northern Britain.
大约1900年前，罗马皇帝哈德良下令在不列颠北部修建一道城墙。
Construction began around AD 122, and the wall ran about 117 kilometers from coast to coast.
工程大约在公元122年开始，城墙从一侧海岸延伸到另一侧海岸，长约117公里。
Small forts were placed roughly every Roman mile, with larger forts holding hundreds of soldiers.
大约每隔一罗马里就设有一座小堡垒，较大的要塞则能驻扎数百名士兵。
Historians still debate its exact purpose.
历史学家对它的确切用途仍有争论。
It may have been less a barrier for battle than a way to control movement and collect taxes on trade.
与其说它是作战的屏障，不如说它可能是用来控制人员往来和对贸易征税的。
Some of the most surprising discoveries came from Vindolanda, a fort just south of the wall.
一些最令人惊讶的发现来自哈德良长城以南不远的文德兰达要塞。
There, archaeologists found thin wooden tablets with handwritten letters, including a birthday party invitation from one officer's wife to another woman.
考古学家在那里发现了写有手写信件的薄木片，其中包括一位军官的妻子写给另一位女士的生日聚会邀请。
Today, walkers can follow a long-distance trail beside the wall's remains, which became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.
如今，徒步者可以沿着长城遗迹旁的长途步道行走，这处遗迹在1987年被列入联合国教科文组织世界遗产名录。
q: Who ordered the wall to be built?
According to historians, what might the wall have been used for?

title: Two Fathoms Deep
photo: Mark Twain Boyhood Home Hannibal / Mississippi River steamboat / Mark Twain portrait
p: Samuel Clemens grew up in Hannibal, Missouri, a small town on the banks of the Mississippi River.
塞缪尔·克莱门斯在密苏里州汉尼拔长大，那是密西西比河畔的一座小镇。
As a boy, he watched the great steamboats arrive and dreamed of working on one.
小时候，他看着巨大的蒸汽船靠岸，梦想着能在船上工作。
As a young man, he made that dream come true and trained as a riverboat pilot.
年轻时，他实现了这个梦想，接受训练成为一名内河船领航员。
On the river, crew members measured the depth of the water and called out the results.
在河上，船员们会测量水深并大声报出结果。
"Mark twain!" meant two fathoms, about 3.7 meters — deep enough for a boat to pass safely.
“Mark twain！”意思是两英寻，大约3.7米——足够船只安全通过的深度。
Clemens later chose this call as his pen name.
克莱门斯后来选用这句喊声作为自己的笔名。
As Mark Twain, he wrote The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, drawing on memories of his river childhood.
他以马克·吐温之名写下了《汤姆·索亚历险记》和《哈克贝利·费恩历险记》，书中取材于他在河边度过的童年记忆。
His humor and his use of everyday American speech helped shape modern American literature.
他的幽默和对美国日常口语的运用，帮助塑造了现代美国文学。
q: What job did Samuel Clemens train for as a young man?
What did the call "Mark twain!" mean?
The water was two fathoms deep
Where did Twain get material for Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn?
His memories of growing up by the river

title: "Mr. Watson, Come Here"
photo: Alexander Graham Bell / Bell telephone 1876 / Bell Homestead Brantford
p: Alexander Graham Bell was born in Edinburgh, Scotland, in 1847, into a family fascinated by speech and sound.
亚历山大·格雷厄姆·贝尔1847年出生于苏格兰爱丁堡，他的家人都对语言和声音充满兴趣。
His mother gradually lost her hearing, and his father developed a system for teaching deaf people to speak.
他的母亲逐渐失去了听力，父亲则发明了一套教聋人说话的方法。
After moving to North America, Bell himself became a teacher of deaf students in Boston.
移居北美后，贝尔本人在波士顿成了一名聋人学生的老师。
His knowledge of how sound travels led him to wonder whether a voice could be sent along an electric wire.
他对声音传播方式的了解，促使他思考人声能否沿着电线传送。
He received a patent for the telephone in March 1876, just ahead of other inventors working on similar ideas.
1876年3月，他获得了电话的专利，仅仅领先于其他研究类似构想的发明家。
A few days later, he spoke into his device and his assistant, Thomas Watson, heard from another room: "Mr. Watson, come here — I want to see you."
几天后，他对着装置说话，他的助手托马斯·华生在另一个房间听到：“华生先生，请过来，我想见你。”
Within a few decades, telephone lines connected cities across the continent.
短短几十年间，电话线就连通了整个大陆的城市。
Bell, however, always considered his work with deaf people at least as important as his famous invention.
然而，贝尔始终认为，他为聋人所做的工作至少和他那项著名的发明同样重要。
q: What was Bell's job in Boston?
What were the first words Watson heard through the telephone, according to the article?
"Mr. Watson, come here — I want to see you."
What did Bell think about his work with deaf people?
It was at least as important as the telephone
It was a waste of time
It was less important than his patent

title: Thunder of Waters
photo: Horseshoe Falls Niagara / Maid of the Mist Niagara Falls / American Falls Niagara
p: Niagara Falls sits on the border between the United States and Canada, where the Niagara River drops on its way from Lake Erie to Lake Ontario.
尼亚加拉瀑布位于美国和加拿大的边境，尼亚加拉河从伊利湖流向安大略湖，在这里跌落而下。
It is actually three waterfalls: the Horseshoe Falls, the American Falls and the smaller Bridal Veil Falls.
它实际上由三座瀑布组成：马蹄瀑布、美国瀑布和较小的新娘面纱瀑布。
The largest, the Horseshoe Falls, is shaped like a giant curve and lies mostly on the Canadian side.
其中最大的马蹄瀑布形如一道巨大的弧线，大部分位于加拿大一侧。
Since the 1840s, boats have carried visitors in raincoats close to the base of the falls, where the roar is deafening and the spray soaks everyone.
从19世纪40年代起，就有船只载着身穿雨衣的游客驶近瀑布底部，那里水声震耳欲聋，水雾会把每个人都淋透。
In 1901, a 63-year-old schoolteacher named Annie Edson Taylor became the first person to go over the falls in a barrel and survive.
1901年，一位名叫安妮·埃德森·泰勒的63岁教师成为第一个坐在木桶里冲下瀑布并生还的人。
Much of the river's water is now diverted to power plants that produce electricity for both countries.
如今，大部分河水被引向发电厂，为两国发电。
Under an agreement between the two nations, more water is allowed to flow over the falls during the day, when tourists are watching, than at night.
根据两国之间的协议，白天游客观赏时允许流过瀑布的水量比夜间更多。
q: How many waterfalls make up Niagara Falls?
What did Annie Edson Taylor do in 1901?
She went over the falls in a barrel and survived
She built the first tour boat
She opened the first power plant
Why does less water flow over the falls at night?
More is diverted to produce electricity
Boats need calm water at night
The lakes are lower at night

title: The Return of the Bald Eagle
photo: Bald eagle in flight / Bald eagle nest / Great Seal of the United States
p: The bald eagle has been the national bird of the United States since 1782, when it was placed on the country's official seal.
自1782年被放上国家国徽起，白头海雕就一直是美国的国鸟。
Despite its name, it is not bald at all; "bald" comes from an old word meaning white-headed.
尽管名字里有“秃”字，它其实一点也不秃；“bald”来自一个意为“白头”的古词。
Not everyone loved the choice: Benjamin Franklin once wrote that the eagle had "bad moral character" and that the turkey was a more respectable bird.
并不是所有人都喜欢这个选择：本杰明·富兰克林曾写道，这种鹰“品行不端”，火鸡反倒是更值得尊敬的鸟。
By the middle of the twentieth century, the eagle was in serious trouble.
到了20世纪中叶，白头海雕的处境岌岌可危。
A widely used pesticide called DDT built up in the fish that eagles ate, causing them to lay eggs with shells so thin that they broke during nesting.
一种被广泛使用的杀虫剂DDT在白头海雕吃的鱼体内积累，导致它们产下的蛋壳非常薄，在孵化时就会破裂。
In the lower 48 states, only a few hundred nesting pairs remained.
在美国本土48个州，只剩下几百对筑巢的白头海雕。
The United States banned DDT in 1972 and protected the birds and their nests by law.
美国于1972年禁用了DDT，并通过法律保护这种鸟及其巢穴。
The recovery was remarkable, and in 2007 the bald eagle was removed from the endangered species list, a symbol of what conservation can achieve.
它们的恢复非常显著，2007年白头海雕被移出濒危物种名单，成为保护工作成效的象征。
q: What does "bald" in the bird's name originally mean?
How did DDT harm the eagles?
It made their eggshells too thin
It poisoned the trees they nested in
It made them unable to fly
The bald eagle was removed from the endangered list
The eagle became the national bird

title: A Gift from a Stranger
photo: Smithsonian Institution Building Castle / National Mall Washington DC / Star-Spangled Banner flag Smithsonian
p: In 1829, a British scientist named James Smithson died and left his fortune to the United States, a country he had never visited.
1829年，一位名叫詹姆斯·史密森的英国科学家去世，把自己的财产留给了美国——一个他从未去过的国家。
His will asked for an institution in Washington "for the increase and diffusion of knowledge."
他在遗嘱中要求在华盛顿建立一个机构，“以增进和传播知识”。
Nobody is quite sure why he made this choice, and Congress argued for years about how to use the money before founding the Smithsonian Institution in 1846.
没有人确切知道他为什么做出这个选择，国会为如何使用这笔钱争论了多年，才在1846年创立了史密森学会。
Today the Smithsonian is a family of museums, research centers and a national zoo, many of them lined up along the National Mall.
如今，史密森学会拥有众多博物馆、研究中心和一座国家动物园，其中许多沿着国家广场一字排开。
Its collections are so large that it is nicknamed "the nation's attic."
它的藏品之多，使它得了个“国家阁楼”的外号。
Visitors can see the Wright brothers' 1903 Flyer, the famous blue Hope Diamond and the huge flag that inspired "The Star-Spangled Banner."
游客可以看到莱特兄弟1903年的“飞行者号”、著名的蓝色希望钻石，以及启发了《星条旗之歌》的那面巨大旗帜。
Perhaps the best part is that entry to its museums in Washington is free, so families can return again and again.
也许最棒的是，它在华盛顿的博物馆免费入场，所以家庭可以一次又一次地来参观。
q: What was unusual about James Smithson's gift?
He had never visited the United States
He asked for a museum in London
Why is the Smithsonian called "the nation's attic"?
It is very old and dusty
What is said about entry to its museums in Washington?
It is open only on weekends

title: From the Cavern to the World
zh: 从洞穴俱乐部走向世界
photo: Cavern Club Liverpool / Mathew Street Liverpool / The Beatles Ed Sullivan Show 1964
p: In the early 1960s, Liverpool was a gritty port city in northwest England whose docks connected it to sailors, goods and records from across the Atlantic.
20世纪60年代初，利物浦还是英格兰西北部一座粗犷的港口城市，码头把它与来自大西洋彼岸的水手、货物和唱片联系在一起。
In a damp basement venue called the Cavern Club, a local band named the Beatles played hundreds of lunchtime and evening shows, sharpening their sound before crowds packed shoulder to shoulder.
在一个名为“洞穴俱乐部”的潮湿地下室场地里，一支名叫披头士的本地乐队演出了数百场午间和晚间演出，在摩肩接踵的人群面前磨砺自己的音乐。
Their raw energy, catchy harmonies and cheeky humor set them apart from the polished pop of the day.
他们原始的活力、朗朗上口的和声以及俏皮的幽默，使他们有别于当时精雕细琢的流行音乐。
On February 9, 1964, the Beatles appeared on The Ed Sullivan Show in New York, watched by an estimated 73 million Americans.
1964年2月9日，披头士登上了纽约的《艾德·沙利文秀》，估计有7300万美国人收看。
The broadcast opened the door to what became known as the "British Invasion," as groups such as the Rolling Stones and the Kinks followed them onto American charts.
这次播出开启了后来被称为“英国入侵”的浪潮，滚石乐队、奇想乐队等团体紧随其后登上了美国排行榜。
Ironically, many of these bands had learned their craft by imitating American rock and roll and blues, so in a sense they were selling America's own music back to it.
具有讽刺意味的是，这些乐队中有许多是通过模仿美国的摇滚乐和布鲁斯来学艺的，所以在某种意义上，他们是把美国自己的音乐又卖回给了美国。
Today, a rebuilt Cavern Club stands on Mathew Street, close to its original site, and Liverpool's waterfront draws music fans from all over the world.
如今，一座重建的洞穴俱乐部矗立在马修街上，靠近原址，利物浦的滨水区吸引着来自世界各地的乐迷。
q: Where did the Beatles develop their sound in Liverpool?
In a basement venue called the Cavern Club
In a recording studio in London
The success of British bands in America after 1964
A war between Britain and America
A TV show about British history
A rule limiting American records in Britain
Why does the author call the British Invasion ironic?
The bands had learned from American music
The bands were not really British

title: Wandering Lonely as a Cloud
photo: Dove Cottage Grasmere / Ullswater Lake District daffodils / Hill Top Beatrix Potter
p: England's Lake District, a compact region of mountains, valleys and glacial lakes in Cumbria, has shaped how the English-speaking world thinks about landscape.
英格兰的湖区位于坎布里亚郡，是一片由山峦、山谷和冰川湖泊组成的紧凑区域，它塑造了英语世界对风景的看法。
Much of that influence can be traced to William Wordsworth, who was born on its edge in 1770 and later lived at Dove Cottage in Grasmere.
这种影响很大程度上可以追溯到威廉·华兹华斯，他1770年生于湖区边缘，后来住在格拉斯米尔的鸽舍。
Together with Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Wordsworth published Lyrical Ballads in 1798, a collection that rejected elaborate poetic language in favor of ordinary speech and deep feeling.
1798年，华兹华斯与塞缪尔·泰勒·柯勒律治共同出版了《抒情歌谣集》，这部诗集摒弃了繁复的诗歌语言，转而采用平实的日常语言和深沉的情感。
His famous poem about a host of golden daffodils was inspired by a walk beside Ullswater with his sister Dorothy, whose own journal described the scene first.
他那首描写一大片金色水仙的名诗，灵感来自他与妹妹多萝西在阿尔斯沃特湖畔的一次散步，而多萝西在自己的日记里最先描写了那番景象。
The Romantic poets helped persuade readers that wild, untamed nature was not something to be feared but a source of spiritual renewal.
浪漫主义诗人们帮助读者相信：狂野、未被驯服的自然不是令人畏惧的东西，而是心灵复苏的源泉。
A century later, the children's author Beatrix Potter used income from her books to buy farms in the area, leaving more than 4,000 acres to the National Trust when she died.
一个世纪后，儿童文学作家比阿特丽克斯·波特用卖书的收入在当地购买农场，去世时把4000多英亩土地留给了英国国民信托。
The region became a national park in 1951 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017, recognized as much for its working farms and cultural history as for its scenery.
湖区于1951年成为国家公园，2017年被列入联合国教科文组织世界遗产名录，它获得认可既因为其风景，也同样因为其仍在运作的农场和文化历史。
q: What was new about Lyrical Ballads?
It used ordinary speech instead of elaborate language
It was the first book printed in Cumbria
It was written entirely by Dorothy
It described cities rather than nature
Who first described the daffodil scene in writing?
How did Beatrix Potter help protect the Lake District?
She bought farms and left them to the National Trust
She founded the national park in 1951
She sold her farms to developers

title: The Rock at the Heart of a Continent
photo: Uluru sunset / Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park / Kata Tjuta
p: Rising about 348 meters above the flat red desert of Australia's Northern Territory, Uluru is one of the most recognizable natural landmarks on Earth.
乌鲁鲁从澳大利亚北领地平坦的红色荒漠中拔地而起，高约348米，是地球上最具辨识度的自然地标之一。
The huge sandstone formation appears to change color through the day, glowing deep orange and red as the sun sets.
这块巨大的砂岩似乎在一天中不断变色，日落时会泛出深橙和赤红的光芒。
For the Anangu, the Aboriginal people of the area, Uluru is not merely scenery but a sacred place woven into Tjukurpa, the law and knowledge that govern their relationship with the land.
对于当地的原住民阿南古人来说，乌鲁鲁不仅是风景，更是一处圣地，融入了他们的“Tjukurpa”——支配他们与土地关系的法则和知识。

European explorers named it Ayers Rock in 1873, after a colonial official, but in 1985 the land was formally handed back to its traditional owners, who lease it to the national park they now manage jointly with the government.
1873年，欧洲探险者以一位殖民地官员的名字将其命名为“艾尔斯岩”，但在1985年，这片土地正式归还给传统所有者，他们再把土地租给如今与政府共同管理的国家公园。
For decades, tourists climbed the rock, even though the Anangu asked them not to.
几十年来，尽管阿南古人请求游客不要攀爬，游客们还是爬上了这块巨岩。
The climb was permanently closed in October 2019, a decision that some visitors resented but that many saw as overdue respect for Indigenous culture.
2019年10月，攀岩路线被永久关闭，一些游客对此心怀不满，但许多人认为这是对原住民文化迟来的尊重。
Visitors now walk the base trail instead, where signs explain stories connected to particular caves and rock features, and some sacred sites may not be photographed.
如今游客改走环绕岩石底部的步道，沿途的标牌讲解与特定洞穴和岩石特征相关的故事，有些圣地则不允许拍照。
q: The Anangu law and knowledge about the land
The name of a hiking trail
The land was handed back to its traditional owners
The rock was named Ayers Rock
How did people react to the closing of the climb?
Some resented it, but many saw it as respect

title: The Stone That Spoke Three Languages
photo: Rosetta Stone British Museum / British Museum Great Court / British Museum Montague House
p: When the British Museum opened in 1759, it was among the first national public museums in the world, built around the vast collection of the physician Sir Hans Sloane.
大英博物馆1759年开馆时，是世界上最早的国家公共博物馆之一，其基础是医生汉斯·斯隆爵士的大量收藏。
Its founding principle — that the collection should be open to all "studious and curious persons" free of charge — still shapes its identity today.
它的建馆原则——收藏应免费向所有“好学和好奇之人”开放——至今仍塑造着它的特质。
Its most visited object is a dark slab of stone found by French soldiers in Egypt in 1799 and handed to the British under a treaty in 1801.
馆内参观人数最多的展品是一块深色石板，它于1799年被法国士兵在埃及发现，1801年根据一项条约移交给了英国人。
The Rosetta Stone carries the same decree written three times: in hieroglyphs, in a script called Demotic and in ancient Greek.
罗塞塔石碑上用三种文字刻着同一份诏令：象形文字、一种叫作世俗体的文字和古希腊文。
Because scholars could read the Greek, the stone became the key to unlocking hieroglyphs, a puzzle that Jean-François Champollion finally cracked in 1822.
由于学者们能读懂希腊文，这块石碑成了破解象形文字的钥匙，让-弗朗索瓦·商博良最终在1822年解开了这个谜题。
Yet the museum's treasures also raise uncomfortable questions.
然而，博物馆的珍宝也引发了一些令人不安的问题。
Many objects were acquired during the height of the British Empire, and countries including Egypt and Greece have asked for some of them to be returned.
许多藏品是在大英帝国鼎盛时期获得的，埃及和希腊等国已要求归还其中一些文物。
The debate over who should own the world's cultural heritage shows no sign of being settled soon.
关于谁应拥有世界文化遗产的争论，看不出会很快平息的迹象。
q: Why was the Rosetta Stone so useful to scholars?
It had the same text in Greek, which they could read
It explained how the pyramids were built
How did the stone come to Britain?
It was handed over under a treaty
British soldiers found it in London
Sir Hans Sloane brought it from Egypt
What controversy does the article mention?

title: Harlem Awakens
photo: Harlem Renaissance / Langston Hughes / Apollo Theater Harlem
p: In the decades after 1910, millions of African Americans left the rural South in what became known as the Great Migration, seeking jobs and escaping racial violence and segregation laws.
1910年以后的几十年里，数百万非裔美国人离开南方乡村，这就是后来所说的“大迁徙”，他们寻找工作，并逃离种族暴力和种族隔离法。
Many settled in Harlem, a neighborhood in upper Manhattan that by the 1920s had become the cultural capital of Black America.
许多人定居在曼哈顿北部的哈莱姆区，到20世纪20年代，那里已成为美国黑人的文化之都。
The flowering of art, literature and music that followed is called the Harlem Renaissance.
随之而来的艺术、文学和音乐的繁荣被称为“哈莱姆文艺复兴”。
Poets such as Langston Hughes wrote in the rhythms of jazz and blues, insisting that everyday Black life was a worthy subject for serious art.
兰斯顿·休斯等诗人以爵士乐和布鲁斯的节奏写诗，坚持认为黑人的日常生活是严肃艺术值得表现的题材。
Zora Neale Hurston, trained in anthropology, collected folk tales and later wrote novels that captured the speech of Southern Black communities.
受过人类学训练的佐拉·尼尔·赫斯顿收集民间故事，后来又写出了生动再现南方黑人社区语言的小说。
The era was full of contradictions.
这个时代充满了矛盾。
At the famous Cotton Club, Duke Ellington's orchestra performed for audiences from which Black customers were excluded.
在著名的棉花俱乐部，艾灵顿公爵的乐团为观众演出，而黑人顾客却被拒之门外。
Even so, the movement gave a generation a new sense of pride and laid cultural foundations for the civil rights struggles that came decades later.
即便如此，这场运动给了一代人新的自豪感，并为几十年后的民权斗争奠定了文化基础。
q: The movement of African Americans from the rural South
The move of jazz clubs to Chicago
A government program to build Harlem
What did Langston Hughes believe about everyday Black life?
It was a worthy subject for serious art
It should be kept out of poetry
It was only suitable for music
It was less important than politics
What contradiction does the article describe at the Cotton Club?
Black musicians played for audiences that excluded Black customers
It was a jazz club that banned music
It was in Harlem but owned by Hughes
It was free but very expensive

title: The Golden Spike
photo: Golden Spike National Historical Park Promontory Summit / Transcontinental Railroad 1869 / Chinese railroad workers Central Pacific
p: On May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit in Utah, a ceremonial golden spike was tapped into place, joining two railroad lines and linking the eastern United States to the Pacific coast.
1869年5月10日，在犹他州的普罗蒙特里峰，一枚具有仪式意义的金色道钉被敲入轨道，将两条铁路连接起来，使美国东部与太平洋沿岸连通。
A telegraph operator sent a single word across the nation: "DONE."
一名电报员向全国发出了一个词：“完工”。
A journey that had taken months by wagon or ship could now be made in about a week.
过去乘马车或轮船需要数月的旅程，如今大约一周就能完成。
The Union Pacific had built westward from Nebraska, relying heavily on Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans.
联合太平洋铁路公司从内布拉斯加向西修建，主要依靠爱尔兰移民和南北战争退伍军人。
The Central Pacific, building east from Sacramento, faced the far harder task of crossing the Sierra Nevada, and it turned to Chinese workers, who eventually made up most of its labor force.
中央太平洋铁路公司从萨克拉门托向东修建，面临的是穿越内华达山脉这一艰巨得多的任务，于是它求助于华工，华工最终占了其劳动力的大部分。
They blasted tunnels through granite in brutal winters and were paid less than white workers, yet they were almost entirely absent from the famous photographs of the celebration.
他们在严酷的冬天炸穿花岗岩开凿隧道，工资却比白人工人低，然而在那些著名的庆典照片中几乎看不到他们的身影。
The railroad transformed the national economy, but it also accelerated the destruction of the great bison herds and the displacement of Native American nations.
这条铁路改变了美国经济，但也加速了大型野牛群的毁灭和美洲原住民部族的流离失所。
In recent years, historians and descendants have worked to restore the Chinese workers' place in the story.
近年来，历史学家和华工后裔一直在努力让华工在这段历史中重新获得应有的位置。
q: What happened at Promontory Summit on May 10, 1869?
Why was the Central Pacific's task harder?
It had to cross the Sierra Nevada
It started later than the Union Pacific
It had no workers at all
It had to cross the Mississippi River
What does the article say about the Chinese workers?
They did dangerous work but were left out of famous photographs
They were paid more than white workers
They built the Union Pacific line from Nebraska
They arrived after the railroad was finished

title: Two Versions of One Treaty
photo: Waitangi Treaty Grounds / Te Whare Rūnanga Waitangi / Waitangi Day waka
p: February 6 is Waitangi Day, New Zealand's national day, marking the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840 between representatives of the British Crown and more than 500 Māori chiefs.
2月6日是新西兰的国庆日怀唐伊日，纪念1840年英国王室代表与500多位毛利酋长签署《怀唐伊条约》。
The first signatures were added at Waitangi in the Bay of Islands, where ceremonial war canoes called waka still gather on the water each year.
最初的签名是在岛屿湾的怀唐伊签下的，每年仍有被称为“waka”的仪式战船在那里的水面上聚集。
Yet the treaty has long been a source of dispute, partly because its English and Māori versions do not say the same thing.
然而，这份条约长期以来一直是争议的源头，部分原因在于它的英文版和毛利文版内容并不一致。

In the English text, the chiefs cede "sovereignty" to Queen Victoria, while the Māori text uses kāwanatanga, a word closer to "governorship," and promises chiefs continued tino rangatiratanga, or full authority, over their lands and treasures.
英文本中，酋长们把“主权”让与维多利亚女王，而毛利文本使用的是“kāwanatanga”一词，更接近“治理权”，并承诺酋长们对其土地和珍宝继续拥有“tino rangatiratanga”，即完全的权威。
Most chiefs signed the Māori version, so many Māori understood they were sharing power, not surrendering it.
大多数酋长签署的是毛利文本，所以许多毛利人理解为他们是在分享权力，而不是交出权力。
In the decades that followed, large areas of Māori land were confiscated or sold under pressure.
此后的几十年里，大片毛利土地被没收或在压力下被出售。
Since 1975, a body called the Waitangi Tribunal has investigated claims of treaty breaches, leading to formal apologies and settlements.
自1975年起，一个名为怀唐伊特别法庭的机构开始调查违反条约的申诉，促成了正式道歉和和解赔偿。
As a result, Waitangi Day is both a celebration and a day of protest and reflection on what the nation's founding promise really meant.
因此，怀唐伊日既是庆祝的日子，也是抗议和反思的日子，人们思考这个国家的建国承诺究竟意味着什么。
q: The signing of a treaty in 1840
The arrival of the first Māori canoes
The end of a war in 1975
Why has the treaty caused disputes?
Its English and Māori versions differ
It was written only in French
It gave all land to the Māori
What does the Waitangi Tribunal do?

title: The Mountains Are Calling
photo: Yosemite Valley Tunnel View / John Muir / Hetch Hetchy Reservoir
p: John Muir was born in Scotland in 1838 and emigrated with his family to a Wisconsin farm as a boy, where his strict father made him work from dawn to dusk.
约翰·缪尔1838年生于苏格兰，童年时随家人移居威斯康星州的一个农场，严厉的父亲让他从早到晚地干活。
After an industrial accident nearly cost him his sight, he resolved to devote his life to studying nature, and in 1867 he set off on a walk of roughly 1,000 miles to the Gulf of Mexico.
一次工业事故几乎让他失明，此后他决心毕生致力于研究自然，并于1867年出发，步行约1000英里前往墨西哥湾。
The following year, he arrived in California and first saw Yosemite, a valley of sheer granite cliffs and thundering waterfalls in the Sierra Nevada.
第二年，他来到加利福尼亚，第一次见到了约塞米蒂——内华达山脉中一个满是陡峭花岗岩峭壁和轰鸣瀑布的山谷。
His essays, which blended scientific observation with almost religious wonder, persuaded many readers that wilderness deserved protection for its own sake.
他的文章将科学观察与近乎宗教般的赞叹融为一体，说服了许多读者：荒野本身就值得保护。

He helped campaign for Yosemite National Park, created in 1890, co-founded the Sierra Club in 1892, and in 1903 camped under the stars with President Theodore Roosevelt, urging him to protect more land.
他协助推动了1890年约塞米蒂国家公园的设立，1892年参与创办了塞拉俱乐部，并在1903年与西奥多·罗斯福总统一起露宿星空下，敦促他保护更多土地。
Not every battle was won.
并非每一场斗争都取得了胜利。
In 1913, despite Muir's fierce opposition, Congress approved a dam in Yosemite's Hetch Hetchy Valley to supply water to San Francisco, a defeat he felt deeply in the final year of his life.
1913年，尽管缪尔强烈反对，国会还是批准在约塞米蒂的赫奇赫奇山谷修建水坝，为旧金山供水，这场失败让他在人生的最后一年深感痛心。
Even so, he is often remembered as the "Father of the National Parks."
即便如此，他仍常被人们称为“国家公园之父”。
q: What led Muir to devote his life to nature?
An accident that nearly cost him his sight
What did Muir do with President Roosevelt in 1903?
He camped with him and urged more protection
He sold him land in Yosemite
He argued for building a dam
He founded the Sierra Club with him
Why was the Hetch Hetchy decision a defeat for Muir?
A dam was approved there despite his opposition
The valley was sold to farmers
